You write one blog article for an online shop from a plan. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, and the plan.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

{"title":"Long Leash for Recall: How to Use a Long Line to Train a Reliable Come","meta_description":"Learn how to use a long leash for recall training: what to look for in a long line, why to clip it to a harness, and simple step-by-step recall drills.","slug":"long-leash-for-recall-long-line-training","markdown":"A long leash for recall, usually called a long line, gives your dog room to wander and make choices while you still hold the other end. That makes it the safest bridge between on-leash walks and off-leash freedom. You can practise the come cue at a real distance, reward every good response and stop a run-off before it starts. Below you'll find what to look for in a long line, why it belongs on a harness, a simple drill plan and tips for handling the line safely.

## Why a long leash makes recall training safer

There's a big gap between a dog trotting beside you on a short leash and a dog sprinting back to you across an open field. On a short leash, your dog never really gets the chance to choose you over a great smell or a passing squirrel. Off leash, one wrong choice can mean a dog heading for a road or chasing wildlife out of sight.

A long line fills that gap. Your dog gets space to explore, sniff and drift away from you, which is exactly when recall matters. If they ignore your call, you can calmly stop them from leaving and help them succeed instead of letting them practise running off. Every time they come back and get rewarded, the habit gets stronger.

That's why we stock a line made for this exact job. The [Training Long Line](P1) is a 30 ft leash made by Northpaw and intended for recall practice [F1, F2, F3, F5].

{{P1}}

## What to look for in a long line for recall

Not every long leash is pleasant to train with. Here's what matters most.

- **Length:** You want enough line to practise real distance, but not so much that it becomes a tangled mess you can't manage.
- **Weight:** A light line drags less on your dog and is easier for you to gather up and let out.
- **Material:** Fabric lines can soak up water and mud, getting heavy and grubby fast. A coated material stays easier to handle in wet grass and puddles.
- **Clip:** The clip takes the strain if your dog hits the end of the line, so it needs to be secure and sturdy. A swivel lets the line turn without twisting up.
- **Handle:** Some lines have a loop at the end and some don't. A line without a loop is less likely to catch on roots or branches when it trails behind a dog.

Here's how our line measures up:

| What to look for | Training Long Line |
|---|---|
| Length | 30 ft [F1] |
| Weight and material | Lightweight biothane [F4] |
| Near water | Floats [F7] |
| Clip | Stainless steel swivel clip [F8] |
| Handle | No handle loop [F6] |

The Training Long Line has no handle loop, so if you like holding a loop at the end, it's good to know that before choosing it [F6]. For the full comparison of shorter leashes and long lines, have a look at our [dog leash length guide](L4).

## Attach it to a harness, not a collar

When a dog hits the end of a long line at speed, all that momentum stops suddenly. On a collar, that jolt goes straight to the neck. A well-fitted harness spreads the force across the chest and body, which makes it the better attachment point for long-line work.

Fit matters as much as the harness itself. A harness that's too loose can slip off, and one that's too tight can rub. You should be able to slide a couple of fingers under the straps, and the harness shouldn't twist or ride up when your dog moves. Our [guide to choosing a dog harness](L3) covers the different styles in more detail.

The [Front-Clip No-Pull Harness](P2) is a harness available in sizes XS, S, M, L and XL [F9, F11]. Across those sizes it fits a chest girth of 13–42 in [F16]. It has four adjustment points, so you can fine-tune the fit to your dog's shape [F13]. A padded neoprene chest plate sits across the front [F14]. Check the [harness size guide](L6) to find the right size before you start.

It also earns its place on everyday walks: the leash ring on the chest turns the dog sideways when it pulls, which helps with dogs who drag you down the street [F12].

{{P2}}

## Step-by-step recall drills on a long line

Recall is built in small, easy wins. Keep sessions short and fun, and move on only when your dog is responding happily at the current level.

### Start somewhere quiet with the line short

Pick a calm space with few distractions, like your garden or an empty corner of a park. Hold the line so your dog only has a little room to move. Wait until they're mildly distracted, then call once in a bright, happy voice.

### Reward generously

When your dog reaches you, make it worth their while. Use high-value treats, a favourite toy or an enthusiastic fuss. Coming back to you should be the best thing that happens on the walk.

### Let out more line and add distance

Once your dog is coming back quickly, let out a bit more line and call from further away. Build up gradually until your dog is responding well at the full 30 ft of the Training Long Line [F1, F5]. If they hesitate, gently guide them in with the line and reward them as if they'd come on their own.

### Add mild distractions

Next, practise in places with a little more going on: a different park, another person nearby, interesting smells. Raise the difficulty one step at a time. If your dog starts ignoring you, go back to an easier setting for a while.

### Keep it positive

- **Call once.** Repeating the cue over and over teaches your dog that the first call is optional.
- **Never call your dog to something unpleasant.** If you need to clip on the short leash to leave, trim nails or give a bath, go and get your dog instead of calling them.
- **Don't always end the fun.** Call your dog in, reward them, then send them back to sniff and play so coming back doesn't always mean the walk is over.
- **End on a success.** Finish each session with an easy recall your dog nails, so they go home feeling great about it.

## Handling the line safely

A long line gives you control, but it needs a bit of care to use well.

- **Keep slack off the ground near your feet.** Loose loops by your shoes are easy to step in or trip over.
- **Never wrap the line around your hands or fingers.** If your dog bolts, a wrapped line can tighten painfully. Hold it in loose folds instead.
- **Consider gloves.** They protect your hands if the line slides quickly through your grip.
- **Only let the line drag in open, safe areas.** A trailing line is handy for practising with less handling, but keep it to wide, quiet spaces away from roads.
- **Watch for tangles.** Keep an eye on the line around your dog's legs, trees, posts and other dogs, and stop to untangle before it tightens.

With no handle loop on the Training Long Line, there's no loop to slip around your wrist, so get used to holding it in a loose fold in your hand [F6]. Because it's made of lightweight biothane, it's easy to gather up and let out as your dog moves [F4]. It also floats in water, so it won't sink out of reach if your dog splashes into a pond or stream [F7].

## From long line back to everyday leash

How do you know your dog's recall is ready for more freedom? Look for a dog who comes back on the first call, in lots of different places, even with distractions around. If that's reliable, you can start letting the line drag more often and holding it less, while still being able to step on it or pick it up if needed. Take it slowly, and go back to holding the line in any new or busy setting.

Even with great recall, a standard leash still belongs in your walking kit for streets, car parks and busy paths where your dog needs to stay close. The [Biothane Leash](P3) is 6 ft long and made of coated webbing that does not absorb water or smell [F17, F18]. It can be wiped clean after muddy walks, which makes it an easy-care partner to the long line [F21]. It has a breaking strength of 600 lb [F22].

{{P3}}

Not sure which length suits which situation? Our [dog leash length guide](L4) breaks it down, and you can find everything for walks and training in our [walking gear collection](L1).

With a long line, a well-fitted harness and plenty of patience, you can build a recall you trust, one happy come at a time."}
